paragraphs: This paper introduces ABC-Boost, a boosting approach for classification problems with multiple possible classes. Its name refers to adapting a base class during boosting. The authors also present ABC-MART, an implementation connected to MART, or Multiple Additive Regression Trees. The contribution therefore includes both a proposed approach and a concrete version built around an established classification algorithm.

The relationship to MART is especially clear in the two-class setting: ABC-MART recovers MART. That gives the new implementation a familiar special case. Its distinguishing contribution concerns classification with more than two classes, where the authors investigate whether the adaptive base-class approach improves the results of the original method.

Evaluation on several public datasets shows improvements over MART for multiclass classification. This is an empirical finding about those evaluations, rather than a claim that every multiclass problem benefits. The paper's practical significance is the extension of a method already used in applications such as web search, while retaining its binary-classification behavior.
icml-2009-abc-boost-adaptive-base-class-.tldr: ABC-MART extends MART through adaptive base-class boosting and improves multiclass results on several public datasets.

paragraphs: Learning a model of an uncertain world does not automatically make planning with it efficient. This paper addresses that gap for relational models, which describe objects and their relationships through probabilistic rules. The starting point is a collection of noisy rules learned from experience; the challenge is using those rules to decide which actions to take.

The authors convert the rules into a structured dynamic Bayesian network. This representation supports reasoning about how the world changes over time. They then use approximate inference to predict the consequences of action sequences. Those predictions provide the basis for planning, connecting a learned relational description to a procedure for evaluating possible future behavior.

The approach is evaluated in online planning within a three-dimensional simulated blocksworld containing an articulated manipulator and realistic physics. The reported experiments show that it can solve problems where existing methods fail. This supports the usefulness of the representation-and-inference combination in the tested setting, where uncertainty and physical interactions make action consequences difficult to predict.
icml-2009-approximate-inference-for-plan.tldr: Converting learned relational rules into dynamic Bayesian networks enables approximate-inference planning that solves problems existing methods fail on in a simulated blocksworld.

paragraphs: Relational classification can require features that combine several statements about objects and their relationships. This paper constructs such features by joining smaller conjunctive blocks, meaning groups of conditions that must hold together. The resulting features are acyclic. The goal is to make richer relational descriptions available to classification through propositionalization, which turns relational information into features.

The key contribution is how the construction process supports pruning. Traditional level-wise methods preserve a monotonicity property related to frequency. The proposed block-wise method instead preserves a form of monotonicity for irreducibility and relevance. These properties concern whether features contain reducible structure and whether they are useful for the classification setting, giving the search different grounds for discarding candidates.

Pruning with these properties allows the method to scale efficiently to features containing tens of first-order literals, the individual logical statements making up a feature. The authors describe this scale as beyond the reach of existing propositionalization and inductive logic programming systems. The significance is a larger practical search space for complex relational features.
icml-2009-block-wise-construction-of-acy.tldr: Building relational features from blocks enables pruning based on irreducibility and relevance, making substantially larger acyclic features tractable.

paragraphs: This paper develops an efficient solver for the multi-task Lasso, a method for selecting variables while learning multiple prediction tasks. Its algorithm repeatedly cycles through blocks of variables and updates them. The authors target problems with thousands of features and tasks, where the cost of finding a solution can become a major obstacle.

The central mathematical result is a closed-form Winsorization operator for least-squares regression with a sup-norm penalty. Having an explicit solution for this operation makes the block updates more efficient. The authors report that the resulting procedure solves very large problems substantially faster than existing methods, extending the coordinate-descent direction established for single-task Lasso.

As a case study, the method selects variables to learn a semantic basis for predicting human neural activation. That learned basis outperforms the standard basis for most test participants and requires fewer assumptions about cognitive neuroscience. The authors also show how it can offer insight into word-meaning representations in the brain. The predictive improvement is explicitly a majority-participant result.
icml-2009-blockwise-coordinate-descent-p.tldr: A closed-form block update accelerates multi-task Lasso and supports learning a semantic basis that improves neural-activation prediction for most test participants.

paragraphs: Hierarchical generative models aim to learn several levels of representation, but applying them to full-sized images creates a scaling problem. This paper introduces the convolutional deep belief network to address that problem. The model learns from unlabeled images and is designed to support realistic image sizes while maintaining a probabilistic account of its hierarchy.

A central ingredient is probabilistic max-pooling, which reduces the size of representations in higher layers in a way consistent with the probabilistic model. This shrinking makes larger images more manageable. The model is translation-invariant and supports efficient inference in both directions: from image evidence toward higher-level representations and from higher levels back toward image-level information.

Experiments with objects and natural scenes show that the system learns useful high-level visual features, including object parts, without labels. The authors also report excellent performance across several visual-recognition tasks and demonstrate inference in both directions over full-sized images. Together, these findings connect scalable representation learning with useful recognition behavior and hierarchical probabilistic reasoning.
icml-2009-convolutional-deep-belief-netw.tldr: Convolutional deep belief networks use probabilistic max-pooling to learn useful visual hierarchies from unlabeled, full-sized images.

paragraphs: A Euclidean projection finds the point in a permitted set that is closest to a given vector. This paper studies that operation for sets used in sparse learning, including the l1 ball and particular polyhedra. These projections act as building blocks inside learning algorithms, so improving their cost can improve a repeatedly used computational step.

The authors recast the two projection problems as finding roots of specially constructed auxiliary functions. This changes the computational task from directly searching for a projected vector to solving a root-finding problem. They show that the resulting problems can be solved in linear time using bisection, compared with the stated O(n log n) worst-case complexity of existing methods.

The paper further exploits the structure of the auxiliary functions to develop an improved bisection algorithm. Empirical studies find the proposed algorithms much more efficient than competing projection methods. The contribution concerns the specified projection problems: their mathematical structure makes it possible to accelerate an operation important to several l1-based sparse-learning procedures.
icml-2009-efficient-euclidean-projection.tldr: Reformulating specific sparse-learning projections as root-finding problems yields linear-time algorithms with strong empirical efficiency.

paragraphs: Listwise ranking methods learn by evaluating ranked lists as a whole. Although these methods had shown strong empirical performance, the authors identify a lack of corresponding theoretical analysis. This paper develops a framework that describes different listwise algorithms and supports reasoning about how their learned rankings may generalize beyond the training data.

The main theorem bounds generalization using the Rademacher average of a class of compound functions. Each compound function combines a ranking model with a listwise loss: the model produces ranking information, and the loss evaluates it. Analyzing this combination makes the bound sensitive to both the prediction family and the way ranking errors are measured.

The authors calculate these complexity quantities for ListMLE, ListNet, and RankCosine. They also examine how tight the bounds are under different list lengths and transformation functions. The contribution is a common theoretical language for assessing these algorithms, including how design choices affect the resulting guarantees. It does not turn prior empirical superiority into a universal ranking-performance claim.
icml-2009-generalization-analysis-of-lis.tldr: A shared theoretical framework provides Rademacher-based generalization bounds for listwise ranking methods, including ListMLE, ListNet, and RankCosine.

paragraphs: This paper learns a kernel matrix using two kinds of information: pairwise instructions about which examples should be similar or dissimilar, and the local geometry of the data. The aim is to obtain a learned notion of similarity that respects supplied guidance while also reflecting how the observed examples are arranged.

The framework jointly models the metric or kernel and the underlying manifold, the geometric structure used to describe the data. For some important parameterized manifold models, the authors show that both the model parameters and the kernel matrix can be estimated efficiently. The algorithm exploits low-dimensional manifold structure and avoids semidefinite programming, supporting the authors' claims of speed and scalability.

The method accommodates a broad class of constraints and is tested on semi-supervised classification, colored dimensionality reduction, and manifold alignment. In each tested task, it performs competitively with or better than the relevant state-of-the-art method. These results support the usefulness of combining geometric information with similarity constraints across several applications, while the efficient-estimation result applies to the specified manifold-model forms.
icml-2009-geometry-aware-metric-learning.tldr: Jointly learning data geometry and a kernel incorporates similarity constraints efficiently and performs competitively across several learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify malicious websites from features associated with their URLs. It uses lexical information about the URL itself alongside host-based information. The application presents two challenges: training data can exceed what batch methods process efficiently, and the features associated with malicious URLs change continually.

The authors investigate online learning, which updates a model as data arrives. This approach fits a setting where both the volume of examples and the evolving distribution matter. To evaluate it, they develop a real-time system for gathering URL features and combine that system with a real-time stream of labeled URLs supplied by a large webmail provider.

The experiments show that the online algorithms studied can match the accuracy of batch techniques, with classification accuracy reaching up to 99% on a balanced dataset. The balanced-data qualification is part of the reported result. The finding supports online learning as a practical way to handle this large, changing classification problem without necessarily sacrificing the accuracy achieved by batch training.
icml-2009-identifying-suspicious-urls-an.tldr: Online learning detects malicious URLs as accurately as batch methods in the reported experiments, reaching up to 99% accuracy on balanced data.

paragraphs: Learning information need not arrive only as labels attached to individual examples. Someone can also provide general constraints describing the desired model. This paper treats both kinds of input as measurements and asks how to learn cost-effectively when several ways of obtaining information are available. The starting point is a model family and a collection of unlabeled examples.

The authors introduce a Bayesian decision-theoretic framework that serves two purposes. It combines diverse measurements already available, and it chooses additional measurements to obtain. This connects model learning with the decision about what information to request next, rather than treating the collection of supervision as a separate, fixed stage.

To carry out inference, the framework uses a variational algorithm that exploits exponential-family duality. The authors demonstrate its merits on two sequence-labeling tasks. The contribution is a unified treatment of different forms of supervision and their selection: example labels and broader constraints become inputs to the same learning-and-decision framework.
icml-2009-learning-from-measurements-in-.tldr: A Bayesian framework combines different forms of supervision and selects new measurements to support cost-effective learning.

paragraphs: This paper concerns learning nonlinear dynamic models, which describe changing systems whose behavior is not captured by a linear relationship. The authors introduce a new learning approach intended to make difficult modeling problems tractable. Its stated scope includes models with long-range structure, so the work addresses dependencies that extend beyond only nearby moments in a sequence.

The theoretical contribution is a consistency result for models with that long-range structure. Consistency provides an asymptotic justification for learning within the setting covered by the theory. This matters because the approach is supported by an argument about its learning behavior, in addition to demonstrations of what it can do on observed data.

The empirical applications involve motion capture and high-dimensional video, two settings where dynamic structure is central to the observations. The authors report results superior to standard alternatives on those applications. Taken together, the theory and experiments support the proposed approach as a tool for nonlinear dynamics with extended temporal structure, with empirical improvements specifically established in the evaluated settings.
icml-2009-learning-nonlinear-dynamic-mod.tldr: A new nonlinear-dynamics learning approach has a consistency result for long-range structure and outperforms standard alternatives on motion-capture and video applications.

paragraphs: This paper presents a common framework for predicting links and edge weights in large networks. Its central idea is to transform a graph's algebraic spectrum, a mathematical representation of graph structure. Different transformations produce different prediction functions, allowing several graph kernels and dimensionality-reduction approaches to be understood within the same framework.

The authors show how to learn the parameters of these functions by reducing parameter estimation to a one-dimensional regression problem. The runtime of that regression depends only on the method's reduced rank. The regression can also be inspected visually, making the learned transformation easier to examine. This efficiency claim concerns the reduced estimation problem rather than every stage of processing a network.

The paper derives variants for undirected, weighted, unweighted, unipartite, and bipartite graphs. Experimental evaluations span social networks, collaborative filtering, trust, citations, authorship, and hyperlinks. This range demonstrates the breadth of settings considered. The central contribution is a shared, efficiently parameterized way to learn spectral prediction functions across different kinds of network data.
icml-2009-learning-spectral-graph-transf.tldr: Learning transformations of graph spectra unifies several network-prediction methods and reduces parameter fitting to a visually inspectable one-dimensional regression.

paragraphs: This paper studies classifiers that use several kernel functions, allowing multiple sources of information to contribute to prediction. A distinguishing choice is that the kernels need not be positive definite. The approach therefore removes an assumption commonly imposed in multiple-kernel learning while still formulating the proposed learning task as a convex problem.

The objective combines a misclassification loss with a mixed-norm regularizer. The loss measures prediction errors, while the regularizer imposes a desired sparsity structure on the solution. Group Lasso is one particular case of this kind of penalty. This gives the framework a way to control structured use of information, alongside its flexibility about the kernels themselves.

The authors solve the objective using proximal minimization algorithms. These are gradient-descent-like procedures designed to accommodate nondifferentiable terms, which arise naturally with sparsity penalties. A numerical simulation on a UCI dataset supports the approach's soundness. The contribution brings together indefinite kernels, structured regularization, and an optimization method suited to the resulting convex but potentially nonsmooth objective.
icml-2009-multiple-indefinite-kernel-lea.tldr: A convex classifier-learning framework combines multiple possibly indefinite kernels with mixed-norm sparsity penalties and proximal optimization.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization is a common approach to collaborative filtering, including predicting movie preferences from rating data. This paper examines probabilistic matrix factorization through a latent-variable perspective. The authors show that it is equivalent to Bayesian principal component analysis, connecting a recommendation method to a broader probabilistic approach for representing data through hidden variables.

That equivalence motivates the next step. The authors consider probabilistic principal component analysis and its nonlinear extension, the Gaussian process latent variable model, as tools for probabilistic matrix factorization. The nonlinear model extends the kind of relationship that the latent representation can express. The paper thus builds its proposed recommendation approach from a conceptual connection between existing model families.

The approach is evaluated on benchmark movie-recommendation datasets, where the authors report performance better than the previous state of the art. This is an empirical result for those benchmarks. Its significance is that the latent-variable reinterpretation leads to a useful nonlinear alternative, linking a theoretical modeling relationship to improved recommendation results in the reported evaluations.
icml-2009-non-linear-matrix-factorizatio.tldr: A connection between probabilistic matrix factorization and Bayesian PCA motivates a Gaussian-process nonlinear model with improved movie-recommendation benchmark results.

paragraphs: Large dense matrices appear in many machine-learning problems, and computing their singular value decomposition can be demanding. This paper examines sampling-based ways to approximate that decomposition. Sampling offers a route to a smaller computational problem, but the choice of approximation method and the information retained from the original matrix both matter.

The authors theoretically compare the Nystrom and Column-sampling methods. Their analysis provides insights into which applications suit each technique, and they follow it with experiments motivated by that theory. This makes the comparison more than a performance contest: it aims to explain differences that can guide the choice of approximation approach.

The paper also proposes an efficient adaptive sampling procedure for choosing informative columns from the original matrix. That procedure outperforms standard sampling methods across a variety of evaluated datasets. The result highlights column selection as a meaningful part of approximation quality. Together, the comparison and adaptive method address both how to construct an approximate decomposition and how to select the data used in it.
icml-2009-on-sampling-based-approximate-.tldr: A theoretical comparison of sampling-based decompositions motivates experiments and an adaptive column-selection method that improves on standard sampling across tested datasets.

paragraphs: Sparse coding represents a data vector using a small selection of elements from a dictionary. This paper focuses on learning that dictionary so its elements fit the data being modeled. Adapting the basis is useful because the quality of the available elements affects how well sparse combinations can represent the observed signals.

The authors propose an online optimization algorithm based on stochastic approximations. It is designed to scale to datasets containing millions of training examples, making dictionary learning practical at a size where repeated batch processing can be demanding. The paper also presents a convergence proof, providing theoretical support for the behavior of the proposed optimization procedure.

Experiments with natural images compare the approach with classical batch algorithms on both small and large datasets. The authors report faster performance and better learned dictionaries. These findings connect the scaling goal to measured improvements in the evaluated image setting: the online approach offers benefits in dictionary quality as well as computational performance.
icml-2009-online-dictionary-learning-for.tldr: An online dictionary-learning algorithm scales to millions of examples and learns better dictionaries faster than classical batch methods in natural-image experiments.

paragraphs: Structured prediction often requires choosing a complex output, making exact inference computationally difficult. Learning systems therefore use approximations, but those approximations can affect the model they learn. This paper studies that interaction and also questions the practice of treating computation as equally costly for every candidate model.

The authors establish risk bounds for max-margin learning when inference uses a linear-programming relaxation. Their analysis characterizes the geometry of the outer polyhedra associated with that relaxation. They also propose a learning paradigm that attempts to penalize hypotheses that take more time to process. This brings inference quality and computational cost into the discussion of what makes a desirable learned model.

The techniques are applied to dependency parsing. The paper provides a compact linear-programming formulation that handles non-local output features and reports a significant improvement over arc-factored models. The application connects the theoretical analysis to a setting where richer relationships among output decisions matter, while the cost-penalization proposal addresses the expense of working with such models.
icml-2009-polyhedral-outer-approximation.tldr: The paper analyzes learning with LP-relaxed inference, proposes penalizing costly hypotheses, and improves dependency parsing with non-local features.

paragraphs: In a partially observable environment, the current observation does not fully reveal the state needed for prediction. This paper introduces Simple Recurrent Temporal-Difference Networks to learn predictions of future observations in that setting. The architecture combines the structure of simple recurrent neural networks with temporal-difference networks to form what the authors call a proto-predictive state representation.

The combination changes how states are represented while retaining the temporal-difference learning strategy for general predictions. The authors explicitly acknowledge a departure from the predictive-representation principle of grounding state representations in observations. This distinction is central to the design: the new architecture keeps the prediction-learning approach while allowing a different internal representation.

Simulation experiments show that these networks can correctly represent states even with an incomplete collection of core tests, also called question networks. In the evaluated environments, this leads to better online learning capacity than temporal-difference networks. The finding supports the usefulness of recurrent structure when the available predictive questions are incomplete, with the improvement demonstrated empirically across the tested environments.
icml-2009-proto-predictive-representatio.tldr: Combining recurrent structure with temporal-difference networks improves online state learning with incomplete core tests in simulated partially observable environments.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with a value function represented as a linear combination of features. Least-Squares Temporal Difference learning estimates the coefficients of those features. When the feature set becomes large, however, the method can fit the available data too closely and become expensive to compute, making feature-rich representations difficult to use effectively.

The authors propose a regularization framework for LSTD, focusing on an l1 penalty. This choice is robust to irrelevant features and also performs feature selection. It therefore addresses the problem of deciding which parts of a large feature representation should contribute to the learned value function, alongside the broader goal of controlling overfitting.

A technical obstacle is that the l1-regularized LSTD solution cannot be written as a convex optimization problem. The paper nevertheless presents an algorithm resembling Least Angle Regression that efficiently computes the optimal solution. Experimental results demonstrate its performance. The contribution combines regularized value-function learning with a practical solution method despite the lack of a convex optimization formulation.
icml-2009-regularization-and-feature-sel.tldr: An l1-regularized LSTD framework selects features and controls overfitting, with a LARS-like algorithm that efficiently computes its optimal solution.

paragraphs: This paper considers ordinal classification, where class labels have an order, under a monotonicity assumption. Increasing the relevant attribute values is expected to move the class label upward rather than downward. The learning problem therefore involves both predicting ordered categories and respecting a specified direction of change between attributes and labels.

The authors formalize learning under these constraints from a statistical perspective and derive a rule-ensemble algorithm. Its first stage uses a nonparametric classification procedure to monotonize the data. Its second stage generates an ensemble of rules consistent with the resulting training set. This separates enforcing the ordered relationship in the data from constructing the rule-based predictor.

The procedure is supported by theoretical analysis and checked in a computational experiment. The contribution gives monotonic rule learning a statistical foundation as well as an explicit construction process. Its relevance depends on the stated modeling assumption: the attribute-to-label relationship should be monotone in the intended direction. Within that setting, the rules reflect the order structure built into the learning task.
icml-2009-rule-learning-with-monotonicit.tldr: A statistically motivated algorithm first monotonizes ordinal data and then builds a consistent rule ensemble.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised support vector machines use both labeled and unlabeled examples. A common approach directly estimates labels for the unlabeled examples, which can be inefficient. This paper investigates whether aggregate information about those labels can provide a more efficient route to learning, focusing on their means.

The authors show a close relationship between an S3VM with known label means and a supervised SVM given all the corresponding labels. This motivates estimating the means first. They propose two versions of meanS3VM that maximize a margin between label means: one uses multiple-kernel learning, and the other uses alternating optimization. The aggregate quantities become central to the learning procedure.

Experiments find that both versions are highly competitive with state-of-the-art semi-supervised learners and sometimes achieve the best performance among the compared methods. They are also more efficient than existing S3VMs. These results support estimating label means as a useful alternative computational strategy, while the stated theoretical relationship is a close connection rather than an assertion that means always replace full label information.
icml-2009-semi-supervised-learning-using.tldr: Estimating label means yields two semi-supervised SVM algorithms with competitive accuracy and greater efficiency than existing S3VMs.

paragraphs: Sparse Gaussian graphical models describe relationships among variables while favoring a limited set of connections. Existing l1-penalized methods encourage sparsity through the precision matrix and allow convex optimization. This paper instead favors blockwise sparse graphs, where the pattern of connections depends on groups of variables.

The authors use a stochastic block model as a prior. Crucially, the groups do not have to be provided beforehand: the approach learns with an unknown block structure. This introduces flexibility in how sparsity is organized, but the resulting optimization problem is no longer convex. The paper develops an efficient variational Bayes algorithm to handle that inference problem.

On motion-capture and gene-expression datasets, the method achieves better test-set likelihood than independent l1 regularization. It can also match group-l1 performance obtained using manually created groups. These findings indicate that learning block structure can improve the fitted probabilistic model while reducing dependence on supplied group assignments. The comparison is supported by the two evaluated datasets.
icml-2009-sparse-gaussian-graphical-mode.tldr: A stochastic-block prior learns unknown group structure in sparse Gaussian graphical models and improves test likelihood over independent l1 on two datasets.

paragraphs: Comparing graphs requires a representation that preserves useful structural information. This paper identifies two shortcomings in existing graph kernels: subgraph-counting methods can lose information about relative positions, while algebraic feature-extraction methods considered by the authors are restricted to graphs without node labels. Both shortcomings limit what a graph comparison can express.

The proposed graphlet spectrum is a collection of graph invariants derived using group representation theory. It captures information about both the number and the positions of labeled subgraphs. The distinction matters because knowing which small structures occur does not by itself describe how they are arranged relative to one another within the larger graph.

Experimental evaluation finds that the graphlet spectrum outperforms state-of-the-art graph kernels. This supports the value of the proposed representation in the evaluated comparisons. The contribution is the combination of label information and positional structure within an algebraically derived system of invariants, providing a richer account of graph structure than subgraph counts alone.
icml-2009-the-graphlet-spectrum-8b94fab6.tldr: The graphlet spectrum captures counts and positions of labeled subgraphs and outperforms state-of-the-art graph kernels in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: A linked document collection contains information about both subject matter and the people producing it. Topic modeling seeks the major themes in the documents, while author-community discovery seeks structure among their authors. This paper argues that these questions are interdependent and should be handled together when analyzing collections such as blogs or research literature.

The authors develop a hierarchical Bayesian model that unifies topic discovery and author-community discovery. Putting both into one framework allows the analysis to account for their relationship instead of treating each as an isolated task. The resulting approach aims to describe what a collection discusses alongside the social organization associated with its authors.

The model is evaluated on two blog datasets from different domains and a CiteSeer research-paper citation dataset. The authors report that these applications demonstrate its effectiveness. The main contribution is a joint modeling perspective on content and author structure, supported by evaluations across both blogs and research literature rather than by a claim that either source of information always determines the other.
icml-2009-topic-link-lda-joint-models-of.tldr: Topic-link LDA jointly models document topics and author communities, with effectiveness demonstrated on blog and research-citation datasets.

paragraphs: Sparse ratings make it difficult to learn recommendation models within a single domain. This paper proposes transferring rating knowledge across related domains through a rating-matrix generative model. The connection between domains is established at the level of implicit user and item clusters, allowing shared rating structure to exist beyond individual users or items.

The model combines a user-item joint mixture model with a cluster-level rating model. A task's rating matrix is described by drawing users and items through the mixture model and drawing their ratings through the shared cluster-level model. This generative account supports filling missing ratings for existing users as well as new users.

A major advantage is that knowledge can be pooled across tasks even when their users and items do not overlap. Relatedness is represented through the shared cluster structure instead of requiring shared identities. Experiments on three real-world collaborative-filtering datasets show that the model can outperform separate models trained for each task. The result supports cross-domain sharing in the evaluated settings without asserting that transfer always improves recommendations.
icml-2009-transfer-learning-for-collabor.tldr: A shared cluster-level rating model transfers recommendation knowledge across related domains even when their users and items do not overlap.
